title: Transcription, Translation, Gene Regulation and Cancer — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Nucleic Acid Metabolism and Gene Expression and Regulation lectures (M. E. Annani-Akollor)

questions.stem: What biochemical product is created during transcription of a protein-coding gene?
questions.why: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase reads one strand of the gene and synthesises a complementary RNA strand. In eukaryotes this primary transcript commonly undergoes processing before translation.

notes.A: A new double-stranded DNA copy is produced by replication rather than transcription.
notes.B: A polypeptide is produced by translation of the RNA message at a ribosome.
notes.C: A collagen fibril forms from processed collagen molecules after protein synthesis.
notes.E: Ribosome assembly requires rRNA and proteins, whereas transcription of one protein-coding gene makes an RNA copy.

questions.stem: In what direction does RNA polymerase synthesize a growing RNA chain?

options.label: C
options.text: From both ends toward the middle

options.label: E
options.text: By ligating amino acids to bases

questions.why: RNA polymerase adds incoming ribonucleotides to the growing transcript's 3′ hydroxyl. Addition at that end makes the nascent chain grow in the 5′ to 3′ direction.

notes.B: The template is read 3′ to 5′, but the complementary transcript extends 5′ to 3′.
notes.C: A transcript has one growing 3′ end, rather than being extended from both ends.
notes.D: Polarity is fixed by formation of each new bond at the transcript's free 3′ end.
notes.E: RNA contains linked ribonucleotides. Amino acids are linked to one another during translation.

questions.stem: Why can RNA polymerase begin a transcript without the primer needed by DNA polymerase?

options.label: A
options.text: It uses DNA ligase as a primer

options.label: C
options.text: It initiates RNA synthesis de novo

options.label: D
options.text: It removes all DNA template bases

questions.why: RNA polymerase can form the first phosphodiester bond between incoming ribonucleotides on a DNA template. This de novo initiation supplies a growing RNA end without a pre-existing primer.

notes.A: DNA ligase seals backbone nicks and does not prime initiation of transcription.
notes.B: The RNA message must be made before ribosomes can translate it.
notes.D: Template bases are retained because they specify the sequence of the nascent RNA.
notes.E: Peptidyl transferase catalyses peptide-bond formation during translation rather than initiation of an RNA chain.

questions.stem: Which DNA segment is most directly involved in specifying the site of transcription initiation?
questions.why: A promoter is a DNA region where RNA polymerase and associated factors assemble. Its sequence and position help determine where transcription starts.

notes.A: A stop codon is interpreted by the ribosome during translation, rather than positioning RNA polymerase.
notes.B: Telomeric repeats protect chromosome ends rather than generally specifying transcript start sites.
notes.C: A splice donor marks an RNA processing boundary near the start of an intron.
notes.D: A polyadenylation tail is added at an RNA 3′ end and does not recruit transcription machinery to a promoter.

questions.stem: What is the function of the bacterial sigma factor during transcription initiation?
questions.why: A bacterial sigma factor associates with core RNA polymerase and helps it recognise promoter elements. The holoenzyme can then position itself to begin RNA synthesis.

notes.A: Spliceosome components catalyse conventional pre-mRNA splicing. A sigma factor instead targets a bacterial polymerase to DNA.
notes.C: Telomerase can extend certain linear chromosome ends. Sigma is a transcription initiation factor.
notes.D: DNA processing enzymes remove Okazaki-fragment primers rather than relying on a transcription sigma factor.
notes.E: Proteases hydrolyse polypeptides, while sigma is involved in recognising promoter DNA.

questions.stem: Which sequence feature is characteristic of many bacterial promoters near the minus-ten position?
questions.why: The bacterial Pribnow box is a promoter element centred roughly ten bases upstream of transcription initiation. Many promoters recognised by the major sigma factor have a TATAAT-like sequence there.

notes.A: A poly-A tail is added to RNA and is not a DNA element upstream of transcription initiation.
notes.B: TTAGGG is a repeat at human telomeres rather than the bacterial minus-ten promoter sequence.
notes.C: AUG is a common translation start codon rather than a promoter motif recognised by sigma.
notes.E: A spliceosome is a eukaryotic RNA-processing complex, not a bacterial DNA sequence.

questions.stem: Which general transcription factor contains TATA-binding protein for RNA polymerase II initiation?
questions.why: TFIID includes TATA-binding protein and associated factors. At promoters containing a TATA box, TBP binds and bends the DNA to help assemble the RNA polymerase II initiation complex.

notes.B: TFIIH contributes to promoter opening and phosphorylation of RNA polymerase II, rather than carrying TBP.
notes.C: TFIIF associates with RNA polymerase II and helps recruit or stabilise it in the initiation complex.
notes.D: TFIIE helps recruit and regulate TFIIH and is not the complex that contains TBP.
notes.E: TFIIB binds the TBP–DNA complex and helps position polymerase, but TBP itself is part of TFIID.

questions.stem: Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase transcribes most protein-coding messenger RNA?
questions.why: RNA polymerase II transcribes nuclear protein-coding genes into precursor mRNAs. Processing of these transcripts produces the mature messages used by ribosomes.

notes.A: RNA polymerase I is responsible primarily for synthesis of the large ribosomal RNA precursor.
notes.B: RNA polymerase III makes molecules such as tRNA and 5S rRNA rather than most protein-coding mRNA.
notes.D: DNA polymerase gamma replicates the mitochondrial genome by synthesising DNA.
notes.E: Bacterial RNA polymerase transcribes bacterial genes. The question refers to the eukaryotic nuclear enzyme.

questions.stem: Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase primarily transcribes the large ribosomal RNA precursor?
questions.why: RNA polymerase I synthesises the large nucleolar precursor that is processed into 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNA in humans. The 5S rRNA is transcribed separately.

notes.A: RNA polymerase II makes protein-coding pre-mRNAs and many regulatory RNAs rather than the large rRNA precursor.
notes.B: RNA polymerase III is used to transcribe 5S rRNA and tRNAs, rather than the precursor of other major rRNAs.
notes.C: DNA polymerase alpha participates in priming nuclear DNA replication and does not transcribe ribosomal RNA.
notes.D: Mitochondrial DNA polymerase copies mitochondrial DNA. Nuclear nucleolar rRNA transcription uses a different enzyme.

questions.stem: Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase commonly transcribes transfer RNA genes?
questions.why: RNA polymerase III transcribes most nuclear tRNA genes in eukaryotic cells. The resulting transcripts undergo processing before they serve as translation adaptors.

notes.A: RNA polymerase I is responsible for transcription of the large nucleolar rRNA precursor rather than tRNAs.
notes.C: RNA polymerase II transcribes most protein-coding pre-mRNAs, not the usual nuclear tRNA genes.
notes.D: DNA polymerase beta is involved in nuclear DNA repair, rather than production of transfer RNA.
notes.E: DNA polymerase gamma replicates mitochondrial DNA and is not the usual tRNA-transcribing enzyme.

questions.stem: How does rho-dependent termination in bacteria stop RNA synthesis?

options.label: A
options.text: A ribosome directly cleaves the DNA promoter

options.label: B
options.text: A spliced intron destroys RNA polymerase

options.label: D
options.text: An RNA-bound helicase releases the complex

options.label: E
options.text: Telomerase caps the growing RNA chain

questions.why: Rho binds the nascent bacterial RNA and uses ATP to move along it. When it reaches a paused transcription complex, it promotes release of the RNA and disassembly of the complex.

notes.A: Ribosomes translate RNA and do not stop this process by cutting promoter DNA.
notes.B: Introns removed by splicing do not mediate the bacterial Rho termination mechanism.
notes.C: Histone acetylation affects eukaryotic chromatin rather than terminating transcription through bacterial Rho.
notes.E: Telomerase adds DNA repeats at chromosome ends and does not cap a bacterial transcript.

questions.stem: Which drug directly inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase?
questions.why: Rifampicin binds the beta subunit of bacterial RNA polymerase. It obstructs extension of very short nascent RNA, preventing productive initiation of transcription.

notes.B: Methotrexate is an antifolate that limits certain nucleotide synthesis pathways rather than directly inhibiting bacterial RNA polymerase.
notes.C: Allopurinol reduces urate formation by inhibiting xanthine oxidoreductase.
notes.D: Colchicine acts on tubulin and alters microtubule dynamics rather than blocking bacterial transcription.
notes.E: Aspirin inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes and does not act directly on the bacterial transcription machinery.

questions.stem: Which toxin is especially potent against eukaryotic RNA polymerase II?
questions.why: Alpha-amanitin strongly inhibits eukaryotic RNA polymerase II, reducing elongation of nascent RNA. This prevents normal production of precursor mRNA.

notes.A: Azaserine inhibits several glutamine-dependent reactions and is not the classic toxin inhibiting RNA polymerase II.
notes.B: Beta-aminopropionitrile inhibits lysyl oxidase, affecting extracellular matrix cross-linking.
notes.D: Allopurinol is used to inhibit xanthine oxidoreductase rather than RNA polymerase II.
notes.E: Aminopterin interferes with folate-dependent metabolism rather than directly blocking transcription by polymerase II.

questions.stem: What is the protective 5-prime cap added to many eukaryotic messenger RNAs?
questions.why: A methylated guanosine is attached to the 5′ end of a eukaryotic mRNA through an unusual 5′–5′ linkage. Cap-binding proteins contribute to stability, export and translation initiation.

notes.A: A polyadenylate tail is normally found at the 3′ end rather than as the 5′ cap.
notes.B: CCA is the mature tRNA acceptor sequence, not the protective cap of an mRNA.
notes.C: A DNA promoter box is a genomic sequence rather than a chemical group attached to RNA.
notes.D: Adenylosuccinate is a purine synthesis intermediate rather than the structure of the RNA cap.

questions.stem: Which processing event removes introns and joins exons in eukaryotic pre-mRNA?
questions.why: The spliceosome uses small nuclear ribonucleoproteins and other components to recognise intron boundaries. It removes the intron and joins the two flanking exons.

notes.A: Replication proofreading removes mismatched nucleotides from growing DNA rather than excising introns from pre-mRNA.
notes.C: Telomerase extends chromosome ends, while splicing acts on an RNA transcript.
notes.D: Ribosomal elongation builds a protein from the coding sequence rather than joining RNA exons.
notes.E: Fibrin transglutamination forms protein cross-links in a clot rather than processing RNA.

questions.stem: Why can a single gene produce multiple protein isoforms in different tissues?

options.label: E
options.text: Permanent conversion of RNA to DNA

questions.why: Alternative splicing produces mature RNAs with different combinations or boundaries of exons from the same precursor. Tissue-specific choices can generate proteins with different domains.

notes.A: Intron removal is part of normal splicing, but the different exon choices are what explain multiple isoforms here.
notes.B: Uniform selection of the same polyadenylation site does not produce different exon combinations.
notes.C: Inhibiting transcription prevents new transcripts from being made to generate the isoforms.
notes.E: Reverse transcription generates DNA from RNA and is not required to produce ordinary tissue-specific splice isoforms.

questions.stem: What is the main protective effect of the eukaryotic 3-prime poly-A tail?

options.label: C
options.text: Replacement of the mRNA coding frame

options.label: E
options.text: Direct initiation of ribosomal RNA synthesis

questions.why: The poly-A tail binds proteins that protect the 3′ end and support efficient use of the message. Shortening of the tail often precedes mRNA decay.

notes.B: Polyadenylation can help form an export-competent mature transcript rather than permanently suppressing its export.
notes.C: The tail lies beyond the usual protein-coding region and does not replace its reading frame.
notes.D: Reverse transcriptase copies RNA into DNA. The protective function of a poly-A tail does not need this reaction.
notes.E: Ribosomal RNA transcription is initiated at appropriate DNA promoters rather than by an mRNA tail.

questions.stem: Which sequence on a mature tRNA accepts an activated amino acid?
questions.why: The mature tRNA acceptor arm ends in CCA. The charged amino acid is esterified to the ribose of the terminal adenosine.

notes.A: A 5′ cap is a modification of many eukaryotic mRNAs, rather than the tRNA amino acid acceptor.
notes.B: A promoter is DNA involved in initiating transcription. It does not accept an amino acid.
notes.D: TTAGGG is a repeat at human chromosome ends and not the tRNA charging site.
notes.E: A TATAAT box is a bacterial promoter feature rather than the RNA terminus modified during charging.

questions.stem: Which molecule catalyses peptide-bond formation in the ribosome?
questions.why: The large ribosomal subunit contains the RNA-based peptidyl-transferase centre. It catalyses transfer of the growing chain onto the amino acid entering the ribosome.

notes.A: Mitochondrial DNA carries genes but is not itself the catalytic part of a ribosome.
notes.B: Collagen fibrils provide extracellular tensile strength rather than catalysing peptide-bond formation.
notes.C: Immunoglobulins are antigen-binding proteins and do not provide the ribosomal active site.
notes.D: The mRNA cap supports translation initiation without directly catalysing each peptide bond.

questions.stem: Which mRNA codon usually initiates translation and specifies methionine?
questions.why: AUG is the usual translation start codon. It is read by the initiator methionine tRNA, which carries formylmethionine at initiation in most bacteria.

notes.A: UAA typically recruits a release factor rather than an initiator tRNA.
notes.C: UGA is a stop codon in the standard genetic code, although specialised recoding can occur.
notes.D: UAG is a standard termination signal, not the usual start of a coding sequence.
notes.E: UUC specifies phenylalanine during elongation rather than serving as the usual initiation codon.

questions.stem: Which codon group functions as signals to terminate translation?
questions.why: UAA, UAG and UGA are the three standard stop codons. A release factor recognises a stop in the ribosomal A site and promotes release of the polypeptide.

notes.A: AUG, UUC and GGA are sense codons for methionine, phenylalanine and glycine in the standard code.
notes.B: GCU, GCC and GCA are synonymous alanine codons rather than stop signals.
notes.C: The two lysine codons and the arginine codon in this set are sense codons.
notes.E: CAU and CAC specify histidine, while CAG specifies glutamine in the standard code.

questions.stem: What is the term for an mRNA triplet recognized by the complementary triplet of a tRNA?
questions.why: A codon is a three-base unit read in mRNA during translation. An amino acid codon is recognised by pairing with the anticodon of a corresponding tRNA.

notes.B: A promoter is a DNA region needed for transcription initiation, not a triplet decoded by a tRNA.
notes.C: An enhancer is a regulatory DNA element that can increase transcription.
notes.D: An operator is a regulatory DNA site that can bind a repressor, rather than a unit of the genetic code.
notes.E: A replication origin is the region where DNA duplication is initiated.

questions.stem: Why is the genetic code described as degenerate?

options.label: A
options.text: A single codon directs two different amino acids

options.label: C
options.text: Several codons can specify one amino acid

options.label: D
options.text: A tRNA anticodon pairs with many unrelated codons

options.label: E
options.text: There are only four total codons

questions.why: Degeneracy means that some amino acids have more than one codon. For example, several triplets differing at their third base can specify the same amino acid.

notes.A: The standard code assigns one main meaning to each codon. Degeneracy is the reverse relationship of multiple codons to one amino acid.
notes.B: Codons of a conventional reading frame are read as successive nonoverlapping triplets.
notes.D: Wobble allows some tRNAs to recognise related codons. It does not mean one anticodon accepts arbitrary triplets.
notes.E: Four distinct RNA bases form 64 possible triplets, rather than limiting the code to four codons.

questions.stem: What determines the effect of inserting a single nucleotide inside a protein-coding region?

options.label: B
options.text: Immediate restoration of all amino acids

questions.why: Inserting one base into a coding sequence changes the grouping of subsequent bases into triplets. This frameshift can alter the amino acid sequence and create or remove a stop signal.

notes.A: An insertion changes sequence length and is not a single-base substitution preserving the amino acid.
notes.B: Downstream codons are regrouped, so the original amino acid sequence is not automatically restored.
notes.C: The changed frame may reach a new stop codon. The original triplet is not guaranteed to be read as a stop.
notes.D: A centromere is a chromosome structure distinct from the reading frame of an individual gene.

questions.stem: What occurs when an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase charges its cognate tRNA?

options.label: A
options.text: An RNA intron is removed from DNA

options.label: B
options.text: An amino acid is linked to tRNA

options.label: C
options.text: A peptide is cleaved from a ribosome

options.label: E
options.text: A codon is transcribed into DNA

questions.why: An aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase activates its amino acid using ATP and transfers it to the matching tRNA. The amino acid becomes esterified to the tRNA's terminal adenosine.

notes.A: Spliceosomes remove introns from RNA transcripts, while a synthetase attaches amino acids to tRNA.
notes.C: Peptide release at a stop codon takes place at the ribosome rather than during tRNA charging.
notes.D: Promoter methylation modifies DNA. The substrate of this reaction is a tRNA acceptor end.
notes.E: Aminoacylation is a covalent attachment reaction and does not copy an RNA codon into DNA.

questions.stem: Which ribosomal binding site holds the growing peptidyl-tRNA during elongation?
questions.why: Before peptide transfer, the ribosomal P site holds the tRNA carrying the growing chain. After transfer to the A-site tRNA, translocation moves the new peptidyl-tRNA into the P site.

notes.A: The A site receives the next aminoacyl-tRNA and can briefly hold peptidyl-tRNA after peptide transfer.
notes.B: The E site is the exit site for tRNA that no longer carries an amino acid or peptide.
notes.C: A promoter is a DNA regulatory element, not a tRNA binding site on the ribosome.
notes.E: Enhancers regulate transcription and do not bind the growing peptidyl-tRNA.

questions.stem: What is the central dogma pathway for expression of a typical protein-coding gene?
questions.why: Transcription copies information from DNA into RNA. Ribosomes then read the coding RNA to determine the amino acid sequence of the protein.

notes.B: Reverse transcription can copy RNA into DNA, but ordinary gene expression does not first copy information from protein to RNA.
notes.C: Translation directly decodes RNA to make protein and does not require a lipid information carrier.
notes.D: Transcription uses a DNA template to make RNA without a carbohydrate intermediate carrying the sequence.
notes.E: Proteins and carbohydrates do not serve as sequential information templates for copying a typical protein-coding gene.

questions.stem: Which bacterial DNA element serves as the binding site for a lac repressor?
questions.why: The lac operator is a regulatory DNA sequence bound by LacI repressor. Occupancy of the operator limits transcription of the structural genes.

notes.A: The promoter recruits RNA polymerase. The lac repressor binds the operator, which is close to or overlaps promoter elements.
notes.B: A terminator specifies where transcription ends rather than serving as the usual LacI binding site.
notes.D: An origin is a site at which DNA replication begins, not the site for lac repression.
notes.E: An enhancer is usually described as a transcription-stimulating regulatory element rather than the specific LacI recognition site.

questions.stem: What is the inducer-linked effect of lactose availability on the lac operon?

options.label: A
options.text: RNA polymerase cannot bind any promoter

options.label: B
options.text: The structural genes are irreversibly deleted

questions.why: Some lactose is converted to allolactose, which binds the LacI repressor. This lowers its operator affinity and favours dissociation, permitting transcription when other conditions are favourable.

notes.A: Allolactose relieves repression and does not prevent RNA polymerase from binding every promoter.
notes.B: The structural genes remain intact. Their expression changes through reversible regulation of repressor binding.
notes.C: The tryptophan repressor regulates a different operon and is activated by tryptophan.
notes.D: The mechanism involves ligand binding to LacI rather than widespread DNA methylation.

questions.stem: Which lac operon gene encodes beta-galactosidase?
questions.why: lacZ encodes beta-galactosidase, which hydrolyses lactose into glucose and galactose. It can also convert some lactose to the inducer allolactose.

notes.A: The lacY product is lactose permease, a membrane transporter that brings lactose into the cell.
notes.C: The lacA product has transacetylase activity rather than beta-galactosidase activity.
notes.D: The lacI product is the repressor that binds the lac operator.
notes.E: trpR encodes the tryptophan repressor and is involved in a different regulatory system.

questions.stem: Which lac operon gene encodes lactose permease?
questions.why: lacY encodes the lactose permease in the bacterial membrane. It couples lactose uptake to proton movement, making intracellular lactose available for metabolism.

notes.A: lacZ encodes beta-galactosidase, which acts on lactose after it enters the cell.
notes.B: The lacA product has transacetylase activity rather than transporting lactose.
notes.C: lacI encodes the regulatory repressor and does not transport lactose through the membrane.
notes.E: The trpR product is the tryptophan repressor, rather than a lactose transporter.

questions.stem: Under which glucose condition does the cAMP–CAP activator most strongly enhance lac transcription?
questions.why: When glucose is scarce, cAMP rises and binds CAP. The complex helps recruit RNA polymerase to the lac promoter, with strong expression requiring relief of lactose-dependent repression as well.

notes.B: High glucose generally lowers cAMP and reduces CAP-mediated stimulation of the lac promoter.
notes.C: Without lactose the lac repressor can occupy the operator, while high glucose also keeps cAMP low.
notes.D: cAMP is synthesised from ATP. Stimulation is linked to glucose availability rather than a complete absence of ATP.
notes.E: CAP activity supports positive regulation, so permanent inactivation would weaken stimulation of transcription.

questions.stem: What is the direct role of tryptophan in repression of the trp operon?

options.label: A
options.text: It binds the lac permease directly

options.label: C
options.text: It acts as a repressor corepressor

questions.why: Tryptophan is the corepressor of the trp operon. Binding to the Trp repressor enables that protein to bind its operator and reduce transcription.

notes.A: Lac permease transports lactose and is part of a different operon's function.
notes.B: Tryptophan acts by regulating repressor binding to DNA. It does not hydrolyse the mRNA.
notes.D: The repression mechanism acts through a bacterial operator and does not require removal of histones.
notes.E: Repression reduces transcription of these genes without permanently disabling the cell's RNA polymerase.

questions.stem: What does attenuation regulate in the bacterial trp operon?
questions.why: Translation of the trp leader peptide influences which stem–loop structures form in the nascent transcript. The resulting switch determines whether RNA polymerase stops early or continues into the structural genes.

notes.A: Mitochondrial DNA replication is unrelated to transcriptional control of the bacterial tryptophan operon.
notes.B: RNA polymerase II functions in eukaryotic nuclei and is not the bacterial enzyme regulated by attenuation.
notes.C: The mechanism relies on coupled bacterial transcription and translation, rather than spliceosomal exon selection.
notes.D: Histone deacetylation regulates chromatin in eukaryotes and does not generate the trp leader terminator.

questions.stem: What is the usual effect of histone acetylation on nearby eukaryotic gene transcription?
questions.why: Histone acetylation reduces the positive charge of lysine side chains and can recruit acetyl-lysine-binding regulators. These effects are usually associated with more accessible chromatin.

notes.A: Acetylation modifies histone proteins and does not delete the associated DNA.
notes.C: Acetylated histones can affect transcription but do not insert a DNA-specific base into mRNA.
notes.D: Ribosomes translate mRNA, whereas this modification acts at chromatin and generally favours accessibility.
notes.E: Histone acetylation does not imply irreversible inhibition of the telomere-extending enzyme.

questions.stem: What is the usual association of methylation at many gene-promoter CpG regions?
questions.why: Methylation of CpG-rich promoter DNA is often associated with transcriptional repression. It can reduce access by some factors or recruit proteins that promote a repressive chromatin state.

notes.A: Addition of methyl groups to DNA is a regulatory modification rather than a mechanism for cleaving histones.
notes.B: Methylation changes the chemical state of a base without adding nucleotides to the template.
notes.C: Promoter methylation is primarily associated with regulation of transcription rather than ribosomal peptide synthesis.
notes.E: Methylation of many promoter CpG regions is linked to lower expression rather than direct activation.

questions.stem: Which chromatin form is typically less condensed and relatively transcriptionally active?
questions.why: Euchromatin is relatively accessible and less compact than heterochromatin. It contains many genes available for transcription, although accessibility does not guarantee that each gene is expressed.

notes.B: Heterochromatin is generally more compact and less transcriptionally active.
notes.C: Metaphase chromosomes are highly condensed as part of mitotic chromosome segregation.
notes.D: A nucleolus supports ribosome biogenesis, and fibrin is a clot protein rather than a chromatin form.
notes.E: The Barr body is a condensed, largely inactive X chromosome and exemplifies facultative heterochromatin.

questions.stem: How can an enhancer influence transcription despite being far from the gene promoter?

options.label: A
options.text: It converts an intron into histone

options.label: D
options.text: It destroys the promoter DNA sequence

options.label: E
options.text: It changes amino acids in the gene

questions.why: DNA can loop so that enhancer-bound proteins contact promoter-associated regulators. This brings distant regulatory sequences into spatial proximity without moving their genomic positions.

notes.A: Introns are nucleic acid sequences, and the enhancer acts through interactions among DNA-bound proteins.
notes.B: RNA polymerase synthesises the transcript. An enhancer can alter its recruitment or activity.
notes.D: Enhancers usually act with an intact promoter and do not require cleavage of its DNA.
notes.E: Altered enhancer activity can change how much RNA is made without changing the encoded amino acids.

questions.stem: What is the advantage of combinatorial transcription-factor control in multicellular organisms?

options.label: A
options.text: Cells express a fixed shared set of genes

options.label: B
options.text: All enhancers require one identical receptor

options.label: C
options.text: RNA polymerase loses all promoter specificity

options.label: D
options.text: Each hormone requires one single unique gene

questions.why: A regulatory region can integrate inputs from several transcription factors. Different combinations of active factors allow the same genome to produce different gene-expression patterns in different cells.

notes.A: Combinatorial control permits cell-type-specific expression rather than enforcing one fixed set of active genes.
notes.B: Different enhancers have different binding motifs and can recruit distinct combinations of regulators.
notes.C: The bound factors help confer regulatory selectivity rather than eliminating promoter specificity.
notes.D: One hormonal signal can affect multiple genes, and each gene can integrate several signals.

questions.stem: Which mechanism changes the abundance of protein without changing transcription of its corresponding gene?
questions.why: Translation can produce different amounts of protein from the same pool of mRNA. Changing how efficiently ribosomes initiate or proceed can therefore alter protein output without altering transcription.

notes.A: Loss of a promoter primarily affects transcription initiation rather than translation of an existing message.
notes.C: Exon deletion changes the gene template and can alter the structure of the encoded protein.
notes.D: An enhancer mutation generally changes regulation of transcription rather than simply changing ribosome activity on a message.
notes.E: Genome duplication changes DNA copy number. It is not a post-transcriptional control of the existing message.

questions.stem: Which process can lower steady-state protein concentration after the protein has already been synthesized?
questions.why: Certain proteins are tagged with ubiquitin chains and recognised by the proteasome for degradation. Faster turnover lowers steady-state protein abundance if synthesis stays the same.

notes.A: Greater DNA polymerase fidelity reduces copying errors, rather than directly removing already synthesised proteins.
notes.B: DNA base-pairing changes act at the level of the genome, not by degrading existing protein.
notes.C: More transcription can supply additional mRNA. It does not itself destroy protein already present.
notes.E: A longer poly-A tail can influence transcript stability or translation rather than directly target existing protein for destruction.

questions.stem: In iron deficiency, which change in ferritin expression helps conserve available iron?

options.label: C
options.text: Complete loss of ferritin coding DNA

questions.why: When iron is scarce, iron regulatory proteins bind an iron-responsive element in the 5′ untranslated region of ferritin mRNA. Translation falls, limiting sequestration of available iron in ferritin.

notes.B: More ferritin would increase iron storage, whereas low iron favours reduced ferritin synthesis.
notes.C: Regulation acts on translation of the existing transcript. The ferritin coding DNA remains available.
notes.D: Cellular iron storage depends on ferritin abundance and is regulated here by translation rather than constitutive secretion.
notes.E: The response is reversible through regulation of an RNA-binding protein rather than deletion of the gene.

questions.stem: How is transferrin receptor mRNA commonly affected by iron deficiency?

options.label: E
options.text: Its protein is converted into ferritin

questions.why: At low iron, iron regulatory proteins bind elements in the 3′ untranslated region of transferrin receptor mRNA. Protection from degradation supports receptor production and iron uptake.

notes.A: Low iron increases stability of the transferrin receptor transcript rather than causing its complete degradation.
notes.B: This response involves regulation of mRNA stability without methylation of the DNA coding region.
notes.D: Stabilised mRNA remains available for translation so the cell can increase receptor availability.
notes.E: Transferrin receptor promotes iron uptake, whereas ferritin is a separate iron-storage protein.

questions.stem: Which alteration most directly converts a proto-oncogene into an oncogene?

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of both copies of a tumour suppressor

options.label: B
options.text: Deletion of a DNA mismatch-repair gene

options.label: C
options.text: Irreversible silencing of normal growth genes

options.label: D
options.text: Increased degradation of a growth-factor receptor

options.label: E
options.text: An activating mutation or gene amplification

questions.why: A proto-oncogene becomes oncogenic when an alteration increases or inappropriately activates its function. Activating mutations and amplification can drive signalling that promotes cell growth or survival.

notes.A: Losing both copies of a tumour suppressor removes a growth restraint, a different mechanism from proto-oncogene gain of function.
notes.B: A mismatch-repair gene defect can increase mutation accumulation, but does not itself activate a proto-oncogene.
notes.C: Silencing removes or reduces a gene's expression rather than converting a proto-oncogene to an abnormally active form.
notes.D: Greater receptor degradation usually reduces the receptor's signalling rather than generating the gain of function described here.

questions.stem: Why can a gain-of-function mutation in one proto-oncogene allele promote tumorigenesis?

options.label: A
options.text: Both gene copies must first be deleted

options.label: B
options.text: One activated copy can drive signaling

options.label: C
options.text: Oncogenes work only after telomere loss

questions.why: An activated oncogene allele can produce an overactive protein or too much of a growth-promoting product. One such allele can be sufficient to increase signalling despite the presence of a normal copy.

notes.A: Deleting both copies is a common way to inactivate tumour suppressors, not a requirement for dominant oncogene activity.
notes.C: Telomere maintenance can affect tumour development, but telomere loss is not required for this gain of function.
notes.D: The activating change increases the gene product's abundance or activity rather than requiring transcriptional suppression.
notes.E: Oncogenic signalling through a gain-of-function protein requires expression of the altered gene product.

questions.stem: What common pattern characterizes tumor-suppressor inactivation within a tumour cell?

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of both functional gene copies

questions.why: Many tumour suppressors follow a two-hit model: both functional copies are lost or inactivated in the same cell. This removes a restraint on growth or survival, although exceptions occur.

notes.A: Activation of one allele is more characteristic of oncogene gain of function.
notes.B: Amplification of a functional tumour suppressor does not directly account for its loss of activity.
notes.C: Additional positive regulatory elements would generally increase gene activity rather than eliminating both functional copies.
notes.E: Increased production of a normal suppressor generally preserves or strengthens its function.

questions.stem: Which transcription factor is commonly called the guardian of the genome?
questions.why: p53 is a transcription factor activated by DNA damage and other cellular stresses. It can trigger arrest, repair-associated responses, senescence or apoptosis, limiting propagation of damaged genomes.

notes.B: c-Myc is a transcription factor that promotes growth and can act as an oncogene when dysregulated.
notes.C: Ras is a small signalling GTPase rather than the transcription factor associated with genome surveillance.
notes.D: Cyclin D helps drive cell-cycle progression through cyclin-dependent kinases rather than coordinating the p53 damage response.
notes.E: E2F is a family of regulators of cell-cycle genes, but the conventional nickname is associated with p53.

questions.stem: What is a direct benefit of p53-mediated cell-cycle arrest following DNA damage?

options.label: C
options.text: Time for DNA repair before division

questions.why: After DNA damage, p53 can induce inhibitors such as p21 that slow cell-cycle progression. The pause gives repair processes time before the cell duplicates or segregates damaged DNA.

notes.A: Checkpoint arrest preserves time to deal with damage and does not require destruction of chromosome ends.
notes.B: Arrest is a regulated response and does not imply permanent cessation of all histone synthesis.
notes.D: Platelet granule release is a haemostatic response, separate from guarding genome integrity in a dividing cell.
notes.E: Cholesterol is made through lipid metabolism and is not produced by converting RNA during arrest.

questions.stem: Which enzyme family executes much of the proteolysis during apoptosis?
questions.why: Caspases are proteases activated in the apoptotic cascade. Executioner caspases cleave selected structural and regulatory proteins to dismantle the cell in an orderly way.

notes.A: Cyclooxygenases make prostaglandin precursors rather than executing apoptotic protein cleavage.
notes.B: Peptidyl transferase forms peptide bonds during translation rather than carrying out proteolysis.
notes.C: DNA polymerases synthesise DNA and are not the proteases that execute apoptosis.
notes.D: Lysyl oxidases initiate extracellular matrix cross-linking rather than cleaving apoptotic substrates.

questions.stem: Which cellular change is more characteristic of apoptosis than uncontrolled necrosis?

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of all plasma proteins before injury

options.label: E
options.text: Rapid diffusion of nuclear DNA from blood

questions.why: During apoptosis, cells typically shrink and form membrane blebs or membrane-bound fragments. Containment of cellular contents helps limit the inflammation associated with uncontrolled rupture.

notes.A: Early cell swelling and membrane lysis are more characteristic of necrotic injury.
notes.C: Extensive membrane rupture releases inflammatory material and is more typical of necrosis.
notes.D: Loss of circulating plasma proteins is not an intrinsic early morphological feature of an apoptotic cell.
notes.E: Nuclear DNA can fragment within an apoptotic cell, but rapid leakage from blood is not the defining morphological change.

questions.stem: What term describes spread of malignant cells to anatomically distant tissues?
questions.why: Metastasis occurs when malignant cells leave a primary tumour, disseminate and establish growth at a distant site. The distant growth derives from the original cancer cells.

notes.A: Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells within a tissue, not the spread of malignant cells.
notes.B: Metaplasia is replacement of one differentiated cell type by another within a tissue.
notes.C: Dysplasia describes atypical, disordered development and does not itself imply distant spread.
notes.E: Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size rather than movement and outgrowth of malignant cells at a distant site.

questions.stem: Why must a growing solid tumour stimulate new blood vessel formation beyond a small size?

options.label: A
options.text: Diffusion alone cannot supply enough oxygen

options.label: B
options.text: Tumour cells have no mitochondrial proteins

options.label: C
options.text: Cancer cells cannot use any glucose

options.label: D
options.text: All malignant cells lose nuclear DNA

options.label: E
options.text: Tumour cells cease all protein synthesis

questions.why: Angiogenic signals such as VEGF help overcome diffusion limits on oxygen and nutrient supply.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a carcinogenic initiator and a tumour promoter?

options.label: A
options.text: Initiators activate antibodies; promoters destroy IgE

options.label: B
options.text: Initiators produce hormones; promoters make collagen

options.label: C
options.text: Initiators cause DNA lesions; promoters drive expansion

options.label: D
options.text: Initiators cause apoptosis; promoters repair DNA

options.label: E
options.text: Initiators block ribosomes; promoters form histones

questions.why: In the classical multistage model, an initiator creates a persistent genetic alteration. A promoter then favours expansion or survival of the altered cells without necessarily directly mutating their DNA.

notes.A: Antibody activation and IgE turnover are immune processes and do not define initiation or promotion.
notes.B: Hormone production and collagen synthesis are not the criteria distinguishing genetic initiation from clonal expansion.
notes.D: Apoptosis removes cells and DNA repair can correct lesions. Promotion instead favours survival or growth of initiated cells.
notes.E: Ribosome inhibition and histone formation do not capture the distinction between causing a lesion and expanding the altered clone.

questions.stem: Which process most directly allows malignant cells to penetrate surrounding connective tissue?

options.label: D
options.text: Decreased cell motility at the border

questions.why: Invasion requires tumour cells to cross basement membrane and surrounding extracellular matrix. Local breakdown and remodelling of these barriers can allow motile cells to penetrate neighbouring tissue.

notes.A: Normal tissue differentiation helps maintain organisation rather than directly allowing a malignant cell to breach matrix.
notes.B: Stronger cadherin-mediated adhesion often helps retain epithelial contacts rather than directly opening a path through basement membrane.
notes.C: DNA proofreading can reduce copying errors but does not remove physical barriers to invasion.
notes.D: Reduced motility would generally hinder movement into connective tissue rather than assisting penetration of the border.
